newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Iraq oil metering station problem said fixable.
newsitem.headline: Iraq oil metering station problem said fixable.

text.p: An oil metering station on the Iraqi-Turkish border needed for a planned "oil-for-food" deal would need about nine months to bring it up to modern technological standards but could be made usable in a matter of weeks, a source at the United Nations said Thursday.

"To bring it up to a modern technological level would take quite a long time, about nine months," the source said. "But it could be used in a matter of weeks -- they could provide some parts which would make it usable. Instead of electronic gauging, readings would have to be taken manually."

The status of the metering station at Zakho was the subject of an unpublished report to the U.N. secretariat from the Netherlands-based Saybolt company, whose experts have been inspecting facilities to be used under a deal permitting the export of $2 billion worth of Iraqi oil over six months to buy food, medicine and other humanitartian supplies to help offset the effects of sanctions in force since Iraq's August 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

The deal, signed by Iraq and the United Nations last May, had been ready to go into effect in September but was delayed when Iraq sent its troops into the largely Kurdish-inhabited north of the country at the end of August to support one side in an inter-Kurdish conflict.
An oil-pricing formula to cover the Iraqi sales also requires the approval of the Security Council's Iraqi sanctions committee, where the United States has yet to give its consent.
Under the "oil-for-food" plan most of the Iraqi oil is to be exported through the pipeline to Turkey, with the rest flowing through the oil terminal at Mina al-Bakr on the Gulf.
